case_study_insert.main_stem: Thornbury Castle Hotel (TCH) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, operating a 60-room boutique hotel near the Dorset coast and employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2007 by Rowan Ashford, it uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and regular staff meetings. TCH plans to invest $780,000 in a new spa and twenty-room annex, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $330,000 retained profit, keeping control with the founder. It has fixed costs of $325,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $120, and produces 12,000 units a year in paid room-nights. TCH faces a labour-turnover problem among housekeeping staff and rising guest complaints about room cleanliness.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The hotel sold 3,100 room-nights last quarter at an average occupancy of 74%, down from 81% a year earlier. Guest complaints rose from 18 to 34 per month, with 62% concerning room cleanliness. Online review score fell from 4.5 to 4.1 out of 5. A staff survey of 40 employees found 55% felt their training was inadequate; on-the-job coaching by senior staff costs $280 per employee while a local college hospitality course costs $1,100 per employee. Laundry delivery averaged 2.6 days.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thornbury Castle Hotel as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.70 to $13.45 per hour from April 2026, raising hotel wage bills. (3) Food, beverage and energy input costs have risen 9.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on domestic short breaks grew 4.3%.

questions.question_text: TCH plans to fund part of its $780,000 spa and annex expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TCH of using the $330,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $330,000 retained profit instead of borrowing avoids interest charges and capital repayments, so TCH's cash flow is protected while it already carries fixed costs of $325,000 a year. Money not paid to the lender can be spent on tackling the housekeeping labour-turnover problem and the guest complaints about cleanliness, helping protect the $120 room price and the 12,000 room-nights sold. Every dollar of interest saved is a dollar available to service the new annex during its first, uncertain months.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and control with Rowan Ashford and the existing private limited company, whereas a larger bank loan could let a lender impose conditions on how the $780,000 spa and annex is operated. Because TCH uses a flat structure with democratic leadership, the founder and staff can decide quickly how to use the new capacity without seeking a bank's approval. There is also no risk of repossession if demand for room-nights falls below the 12,000-unit target, which makes the expansion safer for a 48-employee hotel.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TCH's $330,000 retained profit, $780,000 expansion, cash flow and control.

questions.question_text: TCH wants to fill its new annex. Consider a national tourism-website advertising campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TCH choose to promote the annex? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National tourism-website campaign: Listing the annex on a national bookings portal would put the 60-room hotel in front of travellers planning Dorset breaks, generating bookings quickly. It is costly, however, and TCH would compete with far larger resorts for attention, while commission on each sale reduces the $120 room price received. With $780,000 already committed to the spa and annex, a broad national campaign risks expensive wastage on users who never travel to the coast.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsorship of a local radio station is cheaper and reaches exactly the Dorset catchment that supplies many of the 3,100 room-nights sold last quarter. It suits last-minute and off-peak offers to lift the 74% occupancy. Its weakness is narrow reach; it cannot attract the wider domestic short-break market that grew 4.3%, so it alone may not fill an extra twenty rooms.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the new spa and rooms to precisely the short-break audience identified in the bulletin, at a low cost per booking and with measurable engagement. Results build more slowly than paid advertising and depend on choosing credible influencers, but the hotel's falling 4.1 review score means authentic guest content is valuable.

Recommendation: TCH should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by a small tourism-website listing. Influencers reach the growing short-break segment at low cost and can showcase the spa, while local radio is rejected as too narrow for a twenty-room expansion, and a national campaign is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 48-employee hotel already funding a $450,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States simple promotional ideas with little reference to TCH or its annex.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TCH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of TCH's occupancy, costs and expansion with a justified recommendation that rejects the alternatives.

questions.question_text: TCH's housekeeping labour turnover is high and guest complaints about room cleanliness are rising. Explain two benefits for TCH of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives TCH's 48 employees a real voice in how rooms are cleaned and how the new annex is staffed, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design cleaning checklists and shift rotas are more likely to stay, directly attacking the housekeeping labour-turnover problem and reducing the disruption that contributes to the 62% of complaints about cleanliness. Regular meetings fit the flat structure and give management early warning of problems.

Point 2: Involving housekeeping staff in decisions also produces practical ideas from the people who clean the rooms every day, so standards can be raised without costly outside consultants. Higher commitment should cut the 34 monthly complaints and lift the fallen 4.1 review score, protecting the 74% occupancy and the 12,000 room-nights sold. It also makes the $1,100 college course unnecessary for many workers, saving money while the $780,000 annex beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TCH's turnover, complaints, occupancy and flat structure.

questions.question_text: TCH must improve room-cleanliness standards among its housekeeping team. Consider on-the-job coaching by senior staff or an off-the-job college hospitality course. Which should TCH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Senior housekeepers can demonstrate TCH's own room standards beside the trainee, so learning is directly relevant to the annex and costs only $280 per employee rather than $1,100. Staff stay productive while learning, which protects the 3,100 room-nights sold last quarter and the 74% occupancy. The drawback is that senior staff lose time from their own duties, bad habits can be copied, and there is no formal certificate, which matters if hotel inspectors or online reviewers demand visible standards.

Off-the-job college course: The $1,100 course gives structured, up-to-date techniques and a recognised qualification for the 40 staff surveyed, of whom 55% felt training was inadequate. It removes workers from the floor, reducing short-term room availability when the annex opens, and generic content may not match TCH's exact cleaning procedures, so follow-up coaching would still be required. The total cost for all 40 would be $44,000, affordable beside $780,000 but a real cash outflow.

Decision: TCH should choose on-the-job coaching first, with short college modules for the most senior housekeepers. Coaching is cheaper, machine-and-room specific and avoids taking staff off the floor while labour turnover is already a problem. The full off-the-job course is rejected because $44,000 and lost room time would hurt service just as the annex opens, and coaching can be topped up later.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little reference to TCH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of TCH's costs and service.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in the context of TCH with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TCH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $325,000 ÷ ($120 − $55) = $325,000 ÷ $65 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 room-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $120 − $55 = $65. Answer: contribution per unit is $65.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TCH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 12,000 room-nights to confirm the hotel is comfortably profitable, giving a margin of safety of 7,000 room-nights, which supports going ahead with the $780,000 annex.
2. Use contribution per unit of $65 to model pricing: a $10 discount to $110 would cut contribution to $55 and raise break-even to $325,000 ÷ $55 = 5,909 units, still below 12,000, so off-peak discounts can fill rooms safely.
3. Use the $325,000 fixed costs and $65 contribution to set the sales target needed to service the $450,000 loan, checking the annex can cover its extra fixed costs before committing further spending.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($325,000 ÷ 12,000 + $55 = $82.08 a room-night) each quarter to spot the waste driving the 62% cleanliness complaints and to judge whether the $55 variable cost is rising with 9.2% input inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $65 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 7,000 against 12,000 room-nights; discount modelling at $55 contribution; loan-service volume target for the $450,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $82.08 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TCH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TCH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.14 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $165,000; 2025 current assets = $50,000 + $120,000 + $55,000 = $225,000. 2024 short-term cover = $165,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $225,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.80. The inventory-excluding measure for 2024 = ($165,000 − $40,000) ÷ $110,000 = $125,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.14; for 2025 = ($225,000 − $50,000) ÷ $125,000 = $175,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.40.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened clearly. Cover of short-term obligations rose from 1.50 to 1.80, helped by cash rising from $35,000 to $55,000 and current liabilities rising only from $110,000 to $125,000. The inventory-excluding measure improved from 1.14 to 1.40, so TCH is less dependent on selling stock to pay debts, helpful while it services a $450,000 loan and spends $780,000 on the annex. However, trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up cash; if corporate guests pay late, the stronger position could weaken quickly, and inventories grew to $50,000, so stock control for the new spa should be watched.

Conclusion: TCH's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.50 to 1.80) and the acid test ratio (1.14 to 1.40) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not rely on higher inventory. Rising receivables are the main residual risk, so tighter credit control is advised before the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TCH of introducing dynamic room pricing instead of its fixed $120 price.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Dynamic pricing lets TCH charge more than the fixed $120 price on busy weekends when the annex and spa are full, and less on quiet midweek nights to lift the 74% occupancy. With contribution per unit of $65, a higher peak price adds directly to profit to help service the $450,000 loan, while discounts can fill the 7,000 room-nights of unused margin of safety without changing fixed costs of $325,000.

Disadvantage: Prices that change constantly can annoy guests and damage the 4.1 online review score, especially when those reviews already highlight cleanliness. Competing hotels may undercut TCH, and revenue management takes time from a 48-person team already facing labour turnover; if discounts become the norm, the $120 reference price and the $65 contribution could both be eroded, weakening the case for the $780,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TCH's price, occupancy, contribution and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in input costs will affect TCH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If TCH's $450,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $325,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may also discourage consumers from booking short breaks, but TCH can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.45 per hour): With a workforce of 48, many housekeeping and front-desk roles are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented honestly. The defensible comparison is against given productivity: 12,000 room-nights ÷ 48 staff = 250 room-nights per worker. Unless productivity holds or occupancy rises, unit labour cost climbs and the $65 contribution per room-night is squeezed.

Input cost inflation (9.2% in food, beverage and energy): The $55 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.2%, that adds 9.2% × $55 = $5.06 per room-night, or about $60,750 a year at 12,000 room-nights (12,000 × $5.06). Even a smaller rise would cut contribution well below $65, and this hits every room sold.

Conclusion: The 9.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 room-nights and directly erodes the $65 contribution that justifies the $780,000 annex. The interest rise is only about $3,375 and can be fixed, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains of 250 room-nights per worker, whereas input inflation has no such easy remedy.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TCH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of TCH with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
